extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of history of mathematics; translators/editors of ancient Greek geometry; mathematicians studying Archimedes
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Archimedes' methods of exhaustion (geometrical limiting procedures equivalent to integration) and the specialized Greek terminology he uses for geometric objects and relations. Useful for historians, translators, and mathematicians interpreting Archimedes' proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion via inscribed and circumscribed figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Take both an inscribed figure and a circumscribed figure relative to the curve or surface to be measured, then 'compress' the two figures so that they coincide with one another and with the curvilinear figure; use these to bound the quantity sought and conclude equality by the usual rigorous method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes repeatedly uses paired inscribed/circumscribed constructions (polygons, trapezia, cylinders, sectors) and shows that by increasing the number of parts and diminishing their breadth the inscribed and circumscribed figures can be made to differ by less than any assignable magnitude; he then concludes the area/volume equals the common limiting value. He often proves 'it cannot be either greater or less than' the proposed value rather than invoking modern epsilon-limit language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of equal-sided polygons revolved about diameter to approximate spherical surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribe polygons whose sides AB, BC, CD,... are equal and revolve them about the diameter AA' to produce surfaces; compare the surfaces described by the equal sides to circles of appropriate radii to obtain upper and lower bounds for spherical surface areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes proves proportions such as (BB'+CC'+...):AA' = A'B:BA and uses them to show the surfaces described are less than or greater than certain circles; taking limiting values as number of sides increases yields the true surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing trigonometric summations as Riemann-type sums tending to integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Express areas/surfaces produced by revolving polygonal sides in trigonometric summation form (sums of sines or cosines) and show that as number of terms tends to infinity the sums approach the corresponding definite integrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sums like sin θ + sin 2θ + ... which in the limit correspond to integrals ∫ sin θ dθ; Archimedes' algebraic/trigonometric expressions reduce to modern integral expressions when cos(π/4n)→1 etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume approximation by solids built from inscribed/circumscribed elements (cones/cylinders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the volume of an inscribed or circumscribed solid (built from revolving polygonal sides or assembling cylinders) with the volume of cones or cylinders whose bases equal the relevant surfaces and whose heights are appropriate perpendiculars; use these comparisons to bound and determine the true volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sphere/sector cases he shows the volume of the inscribed/circumscribed figure equals that of a cone with base equal to the surface of the figure and height equal to the perpendicular from the centre to a side; multiplying by appropriate factors (e.g., π/4 etc.) yields the limiting volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cylinder-slicing method for paraboloid segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the axis of the paraboloid segment into n equal parts and approximate the segment by a stack of small cylinders (axes along the segment axis); use inequalities for sums of arithmetic progressions to bound inscribed and circumscribed cylindrical approximations and take the limit as n→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes uses the lemma about sums h + 2h + ... + nh to compare inscribed and circumscribed assemblies of cylinders and thereby deduces the volume relation (segment = 2/3 of circumscribed cylinder or segment = 3 × cone relation), equivalent to performing ∫ x dx.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of arithmetic-progression lemmas to bound sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ elementary inequalities about sums of arithmetic (and arithmetic-squared) progressions — e.g., h + 2h + ... + nh bounds — to obtain upper and lower estimates for discrete sums approximating areas/volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several lemmas are cited (from On Spirals and others) that show bounds like h+2h+...+nh > (n(n+1)/2)h (and corresponding upper bounds). These lemmas are essential when Archimedes replaces continuous integrals by finite sums and then takes limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding via sums of squares and gnomons for spheroid/hyperboloid
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with segments of spheroids/hyperboloids, use sums of squares and differences (gnomons) between rectangles to obtain inequalities and limits corresponding to ∫ (ax - x^2) dx or similar integrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes introduces gnomons (differences between successive rectangles) and proves corollaries about sums of squares (h^2 + (2h)^2 + ... ) to bound the inscribed and circumscribed solids and take the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a spiral by inscribed/circumscribed similar sectors with radii in arithmetic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumscribe and inscribe a spiral by figures made of similar sectors of circles whose radii form an arithmetic progression (h, 2h, ... , nh); use the fact that sectors are proportional to the square of their radii to bound the spiral's area and take limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the first complete turn Archimedes demonstrates (circumscribed fig) > π a^2 and (inscribed fig) < π a^2 (expressed in his notation), concluding area = π a^2 (in his notation jaa'). The same technique applies for partial turns by adjusting the progression endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic segment quadrature via iterative trapezia
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribe and circumscribe trapezia whose parallel sides are diameters of the parabola; show the inscribed figure is less and circumscribed greater than one-third of a certain triangle, then subdivide repeatedly and take the limit to obtain the exact area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes constructs trapezia and proceeds by the usual exhaustion: divide the base, apply the construction to subintervals (obtaining geometric series of triangle areas A, A/4, A/16,...), and conclude the area equals 4/3 of the inscribed triangle area (equivalent to ∫ y dx using the parabola's equation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof strategy: show difference can be made arbitrarily small
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that the difference between inscribed and circumscribed approximations can be reduced below any assigned magnitude by increasing subdivisions; conclude by the 'usual rigorous method' that the common limiting value is the true area/volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the recurring Archimedean logical move: show upper and lower bounds whose difference tends to zero as subdivision refines; Archimedes often phrases it as the figure cannot be greater or less than the predicted value, rather than using modern limit notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology guideline — points and lines (Greek technical terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use σημεῖον for point; a point on a line or curve is σημεῖον ἐπί or ἐν; a straight line is εὐθεῖα or εὐθεῖα γραμμή; a curved line is καμπύλη γραμμή. Use specific locative/prepositional constructions (e.g., ἐπὶ, πρός, διά) as in Archimedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter groups technical terms and shows common phrases: 'a point on a line' ἐπὶ (with gen.), 'a point falling on another' ἐπί or κατὰ with acc., 'the middle point' τὸ μέσον, 'a straight line produced' ἡ ἐπ᾽ εὐθείας. Translator guidance: when explaining single words use ordinary form, but quote Heiberg's text forms where illustrative phrases are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology guideline — particular point and line vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific Greek nouns for particular points and line relations: extremity πέρας, vertex κορυφή, centre κέντρον, point of division διαίρεσις, middle τὸ μέσον; perpendicular κάθετος (with ἐπί), parallel παράλληλος (with dat./πρά), join ἐπιζεύγνυμι, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of usage are provided (e.g., 'let B be its middle point' μέσον δὲ αὐτᾶς ἔστω τὸ B). The text emphasizes idiomatic syntactic constructions (dative/genitive uses) for accurate translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology guideline — angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use γωνία for angle; classify as ὀρθή (right), ὀξεῖα (acute), ἀμβλεῖα (obtuse); adjectives such as ὀρθογώνιος, ὀξυγώνιος denote triangle types; standard locutions for 'angle contained by lines AH, AT' are ἡ γωνία ἃ περιεχομένα ὑπὸ τῶν AH, AT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter expressions are common: 'the angle at O' ἃ ποτὶ τῷ O; Archimedes routinely omits γωνία when context suffices. Note idiomatic verbs and constructions for making angles equal, bisecting, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology guideline — planes and plane figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ἐπίπεδον for plane, ἐπίπεδος (ἐπιφάνεια) for plane surface, τομεύς for sector (or ἐπίπεδος τομεὺς for plane sector), τμῆμα κύκλου for circular segment, ἡμικύκλιον for semicircle, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes distinguishes plane sectors from 'solid sectors' and uses locutions like τὸ ἐπίπεδον τὸ κατὰ τὴν BA for 'plane through BA.' Translators should preserve these distinctions where relevant to geometric arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology guideline — triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangle τρίγωνον; right-angled triangle τρίγωνον ὀρθογώνιον; quadrilateral τετράπλευρον (contrast with τετράγωνον = square); parallelogram παραλληλόγραμμον, diagonal διάμετρος, trapezium τραπέζιον (often 'with two sides parallel').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes uses concise locutions to indicate e.g. 'parallelogram on a straight line as base' ἐπί (with gen.), and has terms for equiangular, equilateral, even-sided polygons (ἰσόπλευρον, ἀρτιόγωνος).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology guideline — rectangles, squares and 'δύναμις' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectangle generally χωρίον (area); to apply a rectangle to a straight line is παραβάλλειν; square is τετράγωνον; δύναμις denotes a square (power) and the dative δυνάμει indicates potential equality (square equal to a rectangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important algebraic/geometric idiom: δύναμις used as 'square' (useful when rendering Diophantine/algebraic language); verb δύνασθαι and forms express 'is equal square to' in geometric statements — translators should preserve 'δυνάμει' constructions to reflect Archimedes' conceptual framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology guideline — circles and circular parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle κύκλος; centre κέντρον; circumference/arc περιφέρεια (used both for whole circumference and for arcs); radius ἡ ἐκ τοῦ κέντρου; diameter διάμετρος; chord expressed as ἡ ἐμπεσοῦσα or ἡ ἐν τῷ κύκλῳ (εὐθεῖα); sector τομεύς; segment τμῆμα κύκλου.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes sometimes uses περίμετρος for perimeter (e.g., of earth) but not generally for circle circumference; note idiomatic phrasing for 'semicircle on ZH as diameter' τὸ ἡμικύκλιον τὸ περὶ διάμετρον τὰν ZH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language/dialect guidance for quoting Archimedes
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes wrote in the Doric dialect, but later editions/transcriptions sometimes transform to ordinary Greek dialects. When explaining single words use the ordinary form; when illustrating use Heiberg's text (Doric or Attic forms) verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator/editor note: preserve original Doric accents/word forms in quotations (Heiberg's text), and make explicit when odd paroxytone forms occur to avoid readers assuming typographic errors. Group technical terms under headings to map Greek terms to modern mathematical phraseology.
